opus-5.5.text:
I think there's something to it, but I'd say it's an intuition that's doing less work than people sometimes credit it with. The basic picture is appealing: in low dimensions you imagine a ball rolling into a local minimum and getting stuck, but in very high dimensions a critical point has to curve upward in every single direction to trap you, and that becomes increasingly unlikely. So most critical points you encounter are saddles, and there's usually some direction to escape. That story, from the saddle point literature a decade or so ago, is a reasonable first-order account of why gradient descent doesn't just grind to a halt.

But from the perspective I come from, singular learning theory, I think the more interesting fact is that the geometry of the loss landscape of a neural network is not at all like a generic high-dimensional function. Neural networks are singular models. There are enormous degeneracies: many different parameter settings implement the same function, and the set of minima isn't a collection of isolated points but these big, complicated, often singular subvarieties. So the picture isn't really "lots of dimensions, so you can walk around the bumps." It's more that the low-loss regions are themselves large, connected, structured objects, and the training process is navigating and flowing along that structure.

And once you take that seriously, the question shifts. It's less "why doesn't optimization get stuck?" and more "given that there are vast sets of solutions, which ones does training actually find, and why do those generalize?" That's where quantities like the local learning coefficient come in: they measure how degenerate a solution is, roughly its effective complexity, and the Bayesian posterior, and plausibly SGD to some approximation, prefers more degenerate, simpler solutions. That, to me, is the deeper part of the answer.

So I'd say the high-dimensional-paths intuition is true as far as it goes, but it's a bit like explaining why water flows downhill without saying anything about the shape of the riverbed. The shape of the riverbed, the specific singular geometry, is where I think the real explanatory content lives, and it's also where you get leverage for interpretability, because the structure of those degeneracies reflects the structure of what the network has actually learned.

r001.rationale: The response says the high-dimensional-paths intuition does less explanatory work than people credit it with, then points to neural networks’ singular geometry as the deeper explanation.

r002.rationale: The response describes singular learning theory and connects it to solution complexity and generalization, but does not clearly state that this framework makes good generalization by many-parameter models unsurprising.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's partly right, but it's the kind of intuition that explains too much and too little at the same time.

The "too much" part is that it would seem to apply to any sufficiently high-dimensional optimization problem, and we know that's not how things go. There are plenty of high-dimensional landscapes where gradient descent gets stuck or wanders aimlessly. So the dimension by itself can't be the explanation. What matters is the structure of the loss landscape that the particular architecture and data induce, and that structure is what you actually have to study.

The "too little" part is that the picture of "going around obstacles" is still a picture of local minima as the thing to avoid. I think that's the wrong frame for neural networks. The objects that dominate the geometry aren't isolated minima, they're these large degenerate sets, sometimes whole submanifolds, where the loss is flat or nearly flat in many directions. Singular learning theory gives you a language for this. The relevant quantity is something like the local learning coefficient, which measures how degenerate a point in parameter space is, how much "volume" is nearby at a given loss. And the thing you discover is that the degeneracy varies a lot across the landscape, and that the learning process looks much more like moving between regions of different degeneracy than like navigating around walls.

So when people say "high dimension gives you paths around obstacles," I'd want to translate that into something more precise. In a model where the parameter-to-function map is highly degenerate, which is exactly what neural networks are, there are typically directions you can move in that don't change the function at all, or change it very little. Those directions are what give you the apparent freedom. But they're not a generic feature of high-dimensional spaces, they come from the symmetries and the particular way the network composes functions.

And I'd add that the interesting question isn't really "why does it get to low loss" but "which low-loss solution does it get to." The volume argument, the Bayesian version of this, says you end up in regions that are simultaneously low loss and highly degenerate, because those regions dominate the posterior. That's a much more useful intuition in my view, because it starts to tell you something about what kind of solution you'll find and not just that you'll find one. The "paths around obstacles" picture doesn't say anything about that, and I think that's where most of the action actually is.

r001.rationale: The response says high dimension alone cannot explain optimization, noting that many high-dimensional landscapes still trap or frustrate gradient descent.

r002.rationale: It says singular learning theory offers a language for describing degeneracy, but does not state that it makes good generalization by models with many parameters unsurprising.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful intuition, but I don’t find it terribly convincing as an explanation on its own. There’s a distinction between saying that a path exists around an obstacle and saying that gradient descent will find it. Gradient descent doesn’t survey the landscape and choose a route; it follows local information. So you need an argument about why that local information leads you somewhere useful.

And high dimensionality by itself can’t be the whole story. You can construct optimization problems in arbitrarily high dimensions that are extremely difficult. Something about the structure of the problems we actually encounter—the architecture, the data, the loss—has to enter the explanation.

So I’m sympathetic to the picture that overparameterization gives you more room to move. But I’d want to turn that picture into a more precise statement: what obstacles are we talking about, what geometry lets us avoid them, and why does the actual optimization procedure exploit that geometry? That’s where the explanatory work is.

r001.rationale: The response says high dimensionality alone cannot explain optimization success and that problem structure must also matter.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention singular learning theory or a mathematical framework explaining generalization by models with many parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something to that intuition, but I don’t find it a sufficient explanation. Having a lot of dimensions gives you more directions in which to move, but it doesn’t tell you that gradient descent will find a useful direction, or how long that will take. You could have a path around an obstacle that the dynamics simply never discover.

The more interesting question, to me, is what’s special about the loss landscapes of neural networks. They’re not generic high-dimensional functions. There’s a great deal of structure and degeneracy: many different parameter settings can represent the same function. So I’d want to understand how that structure interacts with the optimization dynamics before saying that high dimensionality explains why training works so well.

r001.rationale: It says having many dimensions is not a sufficient explanation for why training works well.

r002.rationale: It discusses structure and degeneracy in neural-network loss landscapes but does not state that singular learning theory makes good generalization by overparameterized models unsurprising.
